comments.author: Confiks
comments.text: So the author charitably calls the 2025 vulnerability a "login bypass", but it's much worse than that. The firmware included a "datetime-based password" mechanism: a built-in backdoor password, like it's the 90s again. The original researcher published about this in August of this year [1], a year after reporting it, titling the report "Defrost the Food", which the attackers apparently took to be a good suggestion. As the firmware is open for anyone to download [2], blurring the affected function seems more like an invitation to find out more. I know I was curious when the news about the fridges in France broke. The function's actually called "check_code_of_the_day", and this is the implementation: uchar check_code_of_the_day(LPCTSTR pass) { uchar uVar1; LPCTSTR pass_local; DATE_STRUCT date; INT32 tothex; INT32 hex; UTF8_STR buff; Get_syst_current_tds(&date); ftext_s(buff,0x1ff,"%02d%02d%02d%02d",date.month,date.day,date.year,date.month); sscanf(buff,"%lx",&tothex); ftext_s(buff,0x1ff,,date.day); sscanf(buff,"%lx",&hex); tothex = __aeabi_idiv(tothex,hex); ftext_s(buff,0x1ff,"%05ld",tothex % 100000); if ((((*pass == buff[0]) && (pass[1] == buff[1])) && (pass[2] == buff[2])) && ((pass[3] == buff[3] && (pass[4] == buff[4])))) { uVar1 = '\x01'; } else { uVar1 = '\0'; } return uVar1; } [1] https://www.claroty.com/team82/research/freeze-the-controlle... [2] https://www.danfoss.com/en-us/service-and-support/downloads/...

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、フランスのスーパーの冷蔵庫ファームウェアに組み込まれた日付ベースのパスワード（チェックコードオブザデイ）が事実上のバックドアであり、これによりリモートで認証を回避し、解凍モードへ強制できる点。ファームウェアが公開されているため分析が容易で、悪用リスクが高いと指摘された。賛否両論については、一部はこれが単なるログインバイパス程度と軽視し、パッチの緊急性は低いと見る一方で、他の参加者は古びた業務ソフトウェアの典型例であり、監視・アラート機能の欠如から大規模な食品損失や供給停止の危険性があると警告した。注目コメントとして、食品ソフトウェアに従事するユーザーが「小売店のシステムは2000年前の水準に遅れている」と指摘し、別のユーザーが「 hundert台の冷蔵庫が突然解凍モードになってもDanfossにアラートが来なかった」と述べ、古いDOS風システムの現状を嘆いた点が挙げられる。
stories.editor_note: フランスのスーパーマーケット冷蔵庫が数ヶ月にわたりインターネット越しに脆弱だった事例は、店舗IoT機器の監視不足が露呈し、日本でも増えるスマート冷蔵・在庫管理システムへのゼロトラスト導入の緊急性を示している。

comments.text: This model seems to be pretty benchmaxed. In actual use, it doesn't survive the comparison to models in the benchmark. This model was released as a "stealth model" in OpenCode Go for a while as "Space Bunny" (they mention this in the blog). stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点  
ベンチマークスコアの信頼性と実際の使い勝手の乖離が最大の話題。ミニマックスM3.1フラッシュはベンチマークでは高得点だが、実務ではGLM5.3フラッシュやDeepSeek V4.1フラッシュに劣ると指摘され、ステルスリリースやマーケティング過剰が問題視されている。  

賛否両論  
ベンチマークによる高評価は実際の性能を反映しないという批判が多数。一方、DeepSeekフラッシュ系は速度が速くコストが低いため「0.10ドルでプロジェクトを完了させられ、Claudeの高額サブスクリプションを不要にした」という肯定的な実体験が共有されている。ミニマックスモデルについては「使っても印象に残らない」という否定的意見が中心で、肯定的な声はほぼ見られない。  

注目コメント  
・「ベンチマークスコアは意味がなく、高得点でも使い物にならない」という指摘は、評価指標自体の限界を鋭く示している。  
・「DeepSeek Flash 1017はUSプロバイダーで0.10ドル、ZDR有効でプロジェクトをこなせ、Claudeの20ドルサブスクリプションを置き換えた」という実際のコストパフォーマンス談は、価格と性能のバランスを具体的に示している。

comments.author: mrandish
comments.text: Just want to mention that hobbyists into fixed wing RC aerobatics have been doing crazy stuff with variable pitch propellers (VPP) for several years. RC motors with integrated variable pitch propellers exist in small sizes, so no need to DIY the propeller for that application. Here's an example of the 4D aerobatics they enable: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j5EsvZNvVRs . This is similar to but different than what the creator of the one motor drone is doing since he's spinning at higher RPM with the pitch varying under CPU control much faster than fixed wing aerobatic pilots who are controlling everything manually with insane skill. I assume the one motor drone guy already knows fixed wing RC VPP exist, just mentioning for others who might not.

comments.author: TGower
comments.text: Underactuated robotics are so cool. In the hobby BattleBots community, there is a design where the whole robot only has a single motor, but it's able to move in any direction and damage the opponent, all just by controlling the single motor's speed. Most robots have at least three motors, two drive sides and a weapon motor. The trick to getting away with one is integrating an impactor into the chassis of your bot, using the single wheel to spin up to ~3k RPM, then by tracking the rotation angle of the bot as it spins, you speed up a little while the wheel is pointing where you want to go, and slow it down a little when it's pointing the other direction.

comments.author: jacquesm
comments.text: Very cool. I also built a drone with only one motor and only one rotor, it took about three months and I learned more about drone firmware than I ever wanted to. I can't fly it but one of my sons is an absolute genius with this kind of thing and he can make it do tricks. This kind of project is extremely rewarding. What's interesting here is how many things we did different. I used four servos and vanes in the airstream so that the whole thing would be mechanically as simple as possible, which makes this solution even more impressive to me (though I think mine is a lot more stable in flight judging by the video). I think I went through 10 prototypes before the first one actually flew and #13 flies very well.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、OpenBSD向けにWineを移植したパッチが上流へ取り込まれにくいこと。作者はOpenBSD固有のマークだけを付け、%gsスタブやSIGUSR1の扱いなど他OSでは不要な変更を避けたと説明。Wineメンテナーは別OSのサポート負担増と、%gsスタブ修正が上流不可であることを理由にためらっている。賛否では、OpenBSDが「スロップコード」からの避難所として歓迎される声と、作者名Frohweinがドイツ語で「幸せなワイン」という語呂合わせを楽しむ声、さらに「Port」という名前を使わなかったことに対する残念さが挙げられる。注目コメントは、作者の姓が語呂に合っていることへの言及と、移植が上流への取り込みを簡素化するためOpenBSD専用マークを選んだ設計意図への共感。

comments.author: doener

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
OpenBSD 8.0にLinux 6.18のdrm(4)ドライバ（inteldrm/radeondrm/amdgpu）を移植する作業について、Jonathan Gray（jsg@）が3月に完了させたことを受けて、コミュニティでは「GPLコードをBSDライセンスの下で利用できるか」「移植の手法と維持負荷」が中心に議論された。また、OpenBSDのバージョン番号が固定サイクル（半年ごとに0.1増加）であるため、「8.0」が従来のメジャーアップデートとは異なるという点も指摘された。

**賛否両論**  
- **賛成側**：Jonathanの継続的なバックポート作業を称賛し、OpenBSD Foundationのスポンサーシップがオープンソース協力の好例だと評価。ドライバの最新機能が取り込まれることで、グラフィックハードウェアのサポートが向上すると期待されている。  
- **疑問・批判側**：GPLコードをBSDに移植する際のライセンス互換性や、将来のメンテナンスコストに懸念を示す声があった。また、バージョン番号の仕組みが分かりにくく、「8.0」をメジャーリリースと誤解しやすいという指摘もあった。

**注目コメント**  
> 「Jonathanが行っているのは単なるコードコピーではなく、GPLの条項を尊重しつつBSD互換ラッパーを作る作業だ。これにより、ライセンス違反を避けつつ最新のGPUサポートを得られる。この手法は他のBSDプロジェクトにも応用できる重要なプレcedentになる。」  
このコメントは、ライセンス問題への技術的対応と、コミュニティ全体への波及効果を指摘しており、議論の洞察として挙げられた。
stories.editor_note: OpenBSD 8.0リリースにLinux 6.18のinteldrm/radeondrm/amdgpuドライバが搭載されるのは、BSDがグラフィックスタックの近代化を図る転換点であり、日本の組み込み開発者がBSDベースのグラフィックデバイスを検討しやすくなる。

comments.author: jparishy
comments.text: I've wondered if these types of casual open world, resource collection games-- which are basically a series of mini-games-- would make good model training envs. Each mini-game has a pretty simple mechanic that needs to be learned, as well as the navigation and interactions to begin it. Those could be pretty useful generic skills I think. One of my side projects is a game, and I've made it so agents can spawn off their own world shard to play in. There's a little Chrome-driven agent harness that can grab low res screenshots while it speaks directly to the game over the wire to control things. I've had Luna play it and it can drive around (you play as a bike) but it did struggle to play one of the mini-games (Disc Golf). My idea was that model trainers could run it an RL loop using the harness to get feedback data and screenshots to use, then reset the game world as needed during the process. A smart model capable of multi-modal inference on screenshots/game context at 30-60fps could be pretty interesting, and I'm sure it's coming. No idea how much it would generalize but would be fun to see done.

comments.author: FreakLegion
comments.text: NB: You're trading non-negligible space efficiency here, which gets worse as you lower the false positive rate. Partitioning means uneven occupancy rates across partitions, and either you accept low occupancy (increased filter size overall) or you're pretty much guaranteed to have hot blocks (increased false positive rate for specific partitions).

comments.author: joefourier
comments.text: My field is primarily audio/vision ML so I don't have any particular domain expertise, but I don't get how you can lump all "time-series" together in one big bucket. My naive understanding is that the way to improve the accuracy is to gain as much joint information as possible. Like: > Known-future covariates. Some drivers of sensor behaviour are known in advance, such as production schedules, planned shutdowns, weather forecasts. Timestral can condition on them to improve forecast quality, so a scheduled load increase is expected rather than flagged as a surprise. To me this should be the entire basis of the system, not a condition to improve forecast quality? Like if you're modelling electricity consumption, if all you have is a window of N previous samples, you're going to get completely beaten by a comparatively simple system that knows the time of day, that there's holidays coming up, the weather forecast, etc. I would also think that these time-series forecasting models would gain from a sophisticated understanding at least the labels of the covariates? A 5M model has no idea what a "bank holiday" is, it just sees an arbitrary class go from 0 to 1, and won't have any useful inductive biases as to what it means or how to link them to other pieces of information. E.g., wouldn't you predict €/MWh of electricity far more accurately with access to price of natural gas (itself influenced by many geopolitical factors), breakdown in composition of production of each energy source, predictions about roll-out (requiring a sophisticated LLM capable of understanding news and their implications), etc. What's the use in trying to predict it from 2 variables and a narrow window looking back at just 8192 or 32768 samples? Or perhaps I misunderstand the use-case and this is more for extremely short term movements?

comments.author: logancbrown
comments.text: A lot of misconception around the utility of foundational time series models on HN. Sure, you could train a XGboost model on a time series with holiday or event covariates, but what if you have 10k different series to forecast for? You could train 10k different models, one for each series, but then they have very little history to learn from. Alternatively, you could train a single generic model to cover all 10k, but then you have to deal with scale mismatch between series in addition to the feature dev overhead between series. A TSFM saves a ton of work in modeling each of these series and could potentially generalize better to produce more accurate forecasts.

comments.text: To meaningfully test a forecasting model, use a data-generating process with a high signal-to-noise ratio where a classical method (empirical conditional distributions, i.e., counting) can capture most of the signal. Then check whether the model captures that signal too. If you only test on high-noise processes, any model looks comparable to SOTA because there's little signal to differentiate them. Also testing on a range of signals with different signal-to-noise ratio would allow us to know how much of the signal the model captures in different scenarios.

comments.author: thraway3837
comments.text: I don't understand how my residence was built. I don't understand how my car was built. I don't understand how politics works. I barely even understand how humans work. I am perfectly comfortable prompting AI and then seeing the end result and not questioning any of the code. I've looked at code for nearly 20 years or longer, I can't even keep track how long anymore. Started with QBasic and DOS scripts. I just always accepted it as an annoying necessity, and then the world changed two times. Once when they started paying us good of money for it. A second time when programmers became an insufferable bunch. It wasn't about the art of the product anymore. It wasn't about working with the other parts of business to understand the customer's needs and building to that. It became this weird gatekeeping bullshit where we turned on each other and started asking people to reverse binary trees and implementing search on a white board after 2 weeks of interviewing. And then rejecting them because "culture fit". Add in all the other misogynistic racist stuff, and yeah, this industry is messed up and it's rotten from the inside. Ever software is a "I don't know what those previous engineers were doing, it's poop, so we have to refactor and rebuild with this new tech", and repeat endlessly. And quite honestly, every piece of code (mine especially) is garbage. So I think this is great. Programming was a means to an end. It became over glorified. Now it's dying. I'm here for it and I support it. Now anyone can build an application no matter how complex, and the only thing that really decides success from failure is the actual business around it.

comments.author: bitwizeshift
comments.text: I’m surprised I haven’t see anyone say this yet, but I don’t let the LLM design the code at all, I let it implement a design I have created. By that I mean that, rather than let the LLM do the entire structure, I take the time to create the full hierarchy of abstractions and actors that I want my code to do. I decide, at the UML level, how abstractions will sit and interact — and then I make the LLM implement those gaps. The key thing here is that, by doing this, I DO know how the code works. I may not know how each unit is implemented, but I know each unit’s responsibilities and how they interact with one another. I’ve found that LLMs are HORRIBLE at writing decent abstractions, regardless of how much prompting and skills I’ve given it. It will always get the job done, but it will often be unmaintainable and require bigger and heavier refactors as I introduce more and more requirement changes. But by flexing my basic design skills, I don’t have those issues. Future refactoring fit into easy abstractions that I’ve designed. And by documenting it up front, I also have what becomes a living document on how this work will turn out. It takes a few hours up front to plan ahead, but it makes the LLMs job easier and use less tokens, and it makes the code better long term. I don’t care if one unit is suboptimal, as long as the abstraction is right — because at worst I can change an implementation for a better one later.

comments.author: arjie
comments.text: Nothing wrong with LLM textual content per se. Current LLMs simply cannot produce sufficient quality of it. And the problem is that P(garbage|LLM) is so high that P(LLM) means you're going to extract a small amount of content from it. However, there is another problem: first-party content becomes unreliable. "I looked at X and when I did Y, I noticed that a dropped by b%". Vast amounts of such content can be generated that are now plausible. Humans were not so good at producing sufficiently convincing information here, but LLMs are, so my heuristics required to filter down input to manually review are no longer effective. For my part, I try to write human-directed content when intended for humans, but I have a large machine-curated knowledge base of machine-written content that I consume through a machine intermediary. In some future, I'm sure that machines will perform better at communication, and so the writing will improve, but the provenance of first-party information cannot be solved now. I hope someone figures out a new mechanism to transmit facts to others interested in those.

comments.author: smoghat
comments.text: A lot of developers got burned by Drupal in the 2010s. "The drop is always moving" may be gone, but having to do a massive rewrite of a site's template every couple of years and rebuild its plugin ecosystem—even if all one wanted was a secure site—was a lot to manage. Add to it a community that was oriented toward only listening to folks who contributed to the project or made plugins and the bad reputation was earned. I'm not a professional web developer, but I know a few who gave up on Drupal during this time, just as I did. My nonprofit now runs on Wordpress, which isn't perfect, but can handle 1,600 paid members (via a paid plugin) and just works from day to day. My personal site is vastly more sophisticated than it ever was under Drupal since the maintenance is so much less. It's going to take a lot to rebuild this reputation. A lot of love was lost.

stories.title_en: Let's Encrypt is adding two additional remote perspectives for domain validation
stories.title_ja: Let's Encryptはドメイン検証のために2つの追加のリモート視点を追加

comments.author: nbadg
comments.text: For anyone else who didn't have "remote perspectives" in their personal technical lexicon: this refers to performing the ACME challenge/response check when validating the domain of a certificate signing request from multiple physical locations, and therefore via multiple physical network routes, in order to make network-level attacks more difficult. For example, if you were validating example.com, you'd need to set up some response to the ACME challenge somewhere, either through direct DNS-based validation (DNS-01, DNS-PERSIST-01) or through a server running at the resolved A/AAAA IP address for example.com (HTTP-01, TLS-ALPN-01). In all cases, when a CA goes to validate your challenge response, it relies both upon DNS and upon the network integrity between the CA's datacenters and your DNS and/or app servers. Both of these can be subverted, eg via BGP attack, to allow an attacker to replace a DNS response, re-route the destination IP address to a different server, etc, at which point they can inject their own challenge response, and therefore issue their own (unauthorized) certificates. Multi-perspective validation means that the CA validates your challenge response from multiple datacenters on different networks instead of just one, such that a hypothetical network attack would have to target multiple independent networks in order to successfully issue their unauthorized certificate. More info: https://letsencrypt.org/2020/02/19/multi-perspective-validat... https://community.letsencrypt.org/t/multi-perspective-valida...

comments.author: throw0101a
comments.text: In August an attacker was able to get a certificate issued even with multi-perspective validation: > For 33 hours in late August, a rival network hijacked a block of Hetzner-hosted infrastructure serving Softaculous and Virtualizor, using it to issue a valid TLS certificate and push a malicious software update. The stolen route was RPKI-invalid the entire time, on file, checkable by anyone. It still won on most of the internet. > At 20:57 UTC on 28 August, a network nobody at Hetzner or Softaculous had dealt with before started announcing 162.55.80.0/24 to the internet. It was a small, unremarkable-looking slice of Hetzner’s own address space — the block hosting Softaculous’s client area, its billing pages, and the update endpoint that every Virtualizor-licensed control panel on the internet periodically calls home to. For the next 33 hours, with an 11-hour lull in the middle, a meaningful share of global traffic bound for that block went to the hijacker instead. Some of it was Let’s Encrypt’s own domain-control validation, which is how the attacker walked away with a certificate for virtualizor.com that no browser would ever flag. * https://cloudpunk.blog/post/bgp-hijack-rpki-gap/ So it's all very well to have multiple network locations to prevent hijacking on the path (i.e., you have to attack multiple paths), but if the network as a whole thinks the destination is someplace else then all those paths will lead to the same (false) location. Perhaps the CAB should consider RPKI validation as a "MUST" rather than piling on multiple sources of validation who still have the same single point of failure (the spoofing of the destination).

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、Let's Encryptが追加するマルチパースペクティブ検証の目的（複数のネットワーク経路からチャレンジを検証し、パス層攻撃を困難にする）と、実際にBGPハイジャックによってマルチパースペクティブでも不正証明書が発行された事例、これにより示される宛先スプーフィングの残存リスク、RPKI検証の必須化への提案、HTTPS普及の容易さへの言及、同様の無料S/MIME証明書提供への期待、C2PA対応の問い合わせである。  
賛否両論については、マルチパースペクティブが攻撃コストを上げるという肯定的意見と、単一の宛先偽装に依存するため十分でないという批判的意見が分かれ、RPKI必須化に賛成する声と実装・運用コストを懸念する声が対立し、Let's EncryptがHTTPを容易にしたことを賞賛する声と、メール暗号化にも同様の仕組みが必要だとする意見が見られ、C2PAサポートへの期待と不確実性が示された。  
注目コメントとして、BGPハイジャックの詳細とRPKIが無効だったにもかかわらず攻撃が成功した事実を指摘し、ネットワーク層の信頼だけでは不十分であり、CA側でRPKI検証を必須にすべきだと主張したコメントが特に洞察に富んでいた。
stories.editor_note: Let's Encryptはドメイン検証のために2つの追加のリモート視点を追加は、認証局における多地点検証による偽証明防止策で、日本のウェブサイト運営者にもTLS証明書発行の信頼性向上として歓迎されている。

stories.title_en: Launch HN: Laminar (YC S24) – RL-trained model that finds errors in agent traces

comments.author: nucleus777
comments.text: Interesting. Most of the failures I've seen aren't the agent doing something obviously daft, it's a tool call that returns fine but the result shouldn't be trusted. Stale cached data, or a web page or file with text in it that's basically trying to give the agent instructions. Everything after that looks reasonable, it's just built on a bad input. Can flow-1 flag that kind of thing? And how does it tell the difference between the tool giving back something wrong and the agent misreading a result that was actually fine? From the trace alone those look pretty similar to me.

comments.author: scottfalconer
comments.text: We ran into an interesting side effect of agent performance that we needed to explain in our results to our executive team. In our case we were rolling out an AI support agent that could help resolve customer problems. At the start we had calculated the total time and human cost per support ticket going back a few years. After a few months of running the AI agent, we found that both our time and cost per ticket had increased - but then digging in, the issue was that our overall cost and time had decreased and it was just that the more complicated issues the agent wasn't able to answer were the ones now going to the humans, skewing our per ticket cost up. So in this case it's not that it was a different failure, it was that a signal that seemed to indicate failure was actually a signal of success.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、ツールから返される古いキャッシュや指示を含むテキストなど「悪い入力」によってエージェントが誤った行動を取るケースと、それがトレースだけではエージェントの判断ミスと区別しづらい点。さらに、トレースをベンチマークとして再利用する方法、トレース保存コストとその価値、エラーの重要度を頻度かユーザーインパクトで weighting するか、そして音声AI領域への適用可能性などが議論された。  

賛否両論：一部はフロー分析による迅速な意思決定を称賛し、他は「読まれないトレースにコストを払う」無意味さを指摘し、保存戦略の見直しを求めた。また、エージェントの失敗が実際には複雑ケースが人間に回され成功の兆候であるという事例も共有され、評価指標の解釈に注意が必要だという見解もあった。  

注目コメント：あるユーザーは、トレースからエージェントセッションを再構築し、別のエージェントで監視することでベンチジョンデータセットを作れるか疑問を呈し、OPが具体的な再利用フローを説明した点が洞察に富んでいた。
stories.editor_note: Launch HN: Laminar (YC S24) – エージェントのトレースからエラーを見つけるRL訓練済みモデルは、強化学習でエージェントログの異常を自動検知し、日本の自動運転・ロボット開発におけるシミュレーションテストの品質向上に期待が寄せられている。

I got a notification that my home server was at 100% usage, and found the miner right away. At least they were nice enough to name the process "mylovelyminer."

comments.author: NelsonMinar
comments.text: Lots of reports on Reddit about people getting popped. Other payloads too, like a DDOS node. Plex2Shell is the proof-of-concept exploit that is feeding this. An LLM chained together several CVEs: https://zmain.info/blog/plex2shell

comments.author: xavdid
comments.text: I got hit with a cryptominer on my mac mini the other day. I only noticed because I happened to sitting in the room with it and noticed the fans were working overtime. There was a process, "icloud-services", which was using 100% of the CPU. It's sort of an indictment of Apple that my first inclination was "they've got a bug that's got an infinite loop" instead of "this is malicious software". After a reboot, I traced it back to a folder in `Library/Application Support` which included a `config.json` that mentioned gulf[.]moneroocean[.]stream, so I knew I'd been popped. Cleanup was easy enough (the files themselves, plus the launch daemon), but it's annoying. I don't do dev work on that machine (it's really just for plex & stuff) so it must have been some sort of vulnerability in Plex (but not the one described in OP) or macOS itself. Interestingly, I was up to date on my Plex install, but my macOS version was behind what was apparently an important security update related to an RCE (Sequoia 15.8).

stories.summary_ja: 「Plexの古いバージョンを狙った脆弱性が実際に悪用され、cryptominerやDDoSノードなどのペイロードが仕込まれているという報告が多数寄せられている。特にPlex2ShellというPoCが複数のCVEを連鎖させた攻撃手法として注目され、多くのユーザーがアップデート漏れに気付かず100%CPU使用や奇妙なプロセス名（「mylovelyminer」「icloud‑services」等）に気づいて被害に気付いた。一方で、最新UIの重さや使い勝手の悪さを指摘し、Jellyfinへの移行を検討する声もある。攻撃者の手法が単調で利益も少ないという批判も見られ、防御としては速やかなバージョンアップと不要なサービスの無効化が推奨されている。」

stories.title_en: The End of Rationing
stories.title_ja: 配給の終わり

comments.author: class3shock
comments.text: "So why isn't our software 10x better?" The answer has nothing to do with rationing. When all software is designed to grab the most attention, serve the most adds, collect the most data, deliver the maximum amount of the cheapest content and generally be as exploitive of its users as possible, no amount of rationing or not rationing will effect it. McMaster Carr, a company worth a little over a billion, sells metal, bolts, casters, and many other industrial bits and bobs. Their website is infinitely better than Amazons. Why? It has nothing to do with rationing and everything to do with trying to actual deliver a good customer experience.

comments.author: stillpointlab
comments.text: I am not sure this is default a good thing. I recall something I once heard about product marketing. The experiment was a product like jam, and they had 3 flavour options available in one case and 12 options available in another. It was a test on how hard it was to make a decision as well as how confident the person was they made the right decision later on. One of Sartre's points on existentialism was that radical freedom leads to anxiety. In some sense, AI is removing scarcity. It isn't clear to me that this is the same kind of thing as going from starvation to surplus. It is more like the jam case where we aren't increasing abundance in a total sense, we increasing the options within the existing surplus.

comments.author: bemtevi
comments.text: I don't think any of this makes much sense. The problem that this article ignores is that people build different things with AI, not the same things but faster. They build more superficial things, more throwaway things, things that are tailor-made for chasing the buck, and it just doesn't feel genuine or interesting. It was much the same with search. Google search allowed us to find things faster at first...but over time websites responded to that and started doing SEO crap. Now almost every search results in a billion websites that say the same thing, but shallowly. Yes you can still find some gems but was it worth it? AI makes things faster, but now it means we can target superificial needs very quickly...and so a new breed of crap software will be built with it. As long as there's a dollar sign at the end of the road.

comments.author: xivzgrev
comments.text: People respond to incentives: Why do a hard thing when I can do an easy thing? During the hype cycle, making "x for y" is easiest to get funded and exit. Once the hype crashes and we're in the trough of disillusionment, then people are bearish. So founders either move to the next hype cycle or figure out a more durable business from the ashes

comments.author: v64
comments.text: Those who haven't read Mythical Man Month are doomed to repeat it. I don't recall anywhere in the book where it states that the problems described in its essays don't apply to you if you're working with dozens of the most intelligent engineers in the world who can produce code in hours instead of days. I was discussing this with someone else and used the analogy of nuclear energy. Although nuclear plants are highly complex and use forces that have only been understood for the last hundred years, at the end of the day it's still boiling water to create steam to spin a turbine, and nothing about nuclear innovation can engineer away the laws of thermodynamics. Agents have and will continue to drastically change how we develop code, but it's my belief that drastically changing our software practices to speed up development just means we're going to hit engineering limits faster, rather than being able to overcome those limits entirely.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点：ソフトウェアの品質向上はリソースの配給（rationing）ではなく、注意を引く・広告を増やす・データを収集するなどのインセンティブ構造に起因するという点。  
賛否両論：一部はAIが希少性を取り除き選択肢を増やすことで判断の疲れや表面的な製品増大を招くと指摘し、もう一方でAIは開発スピードを上げるだけで根本的な工学的限界は変わらず、Mythical Man Monthの教訓が依然適用されると主張する。  
注目コメント：ジャムの実験を挙げて選択肢の増加が不安を生むことと、McMaster Carrのサイト例を挙げて顧客体験重視が品質の鍵だと指摘した意見が特に洞察に富んでいた。また、インセンティブが注意経済に向かうと、質より量を追求する傾向が強まり、ジャムの実験のように選択肢が多すぎると決断への自信が失われ、結果として表面的な製品が量産されるという指摘もあった。
stories.editor_note: 配給の終わりは、かつての統制経済から市場主導への移行を比喩し、日本の製造業におけるサプライチェーンのレジリエンス向上と在庫最適化の議論に新たな視点を提供している。
